knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_torto: When approaching walls or coming under missile fire, Roman soldiers could overlap their shields into a testudo. The protection came at a cost: slower movement, poorer visibility, and little room for close combat, while the formation depended on suitable ground and tight order. It suited particular situations; it was no all-day, invulnerable shell.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_pilum: Legionaries often threw heavy pila before close combat. The long iron shank could drive the point through a shield, leaving the weapon dangling and cumbersome. Surviving examples vary in construction, so the familiar claim that every pilum was built to bend automatically on impact is too absolute.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_vindo: Roman segmented armour was built from groups of curved iron strips, joined by hinges, buckles, and internal leather straps. Finds from Corbridge in Britain allowed researchers to reconstruct the design in much greater detail. The plates could move with the body, but the whole system relied on many small fittings that could break or come loose.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_milit: Some veterans of auxiliary units and fleets received military diplomas at the end of their service, inscribed on two bronze plates. The text copied the emperor's grant and named the unit and veteran, sometimes including family members. It carried honour, but also served as durable legal proof of identity and citizenship.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_hobna: Romans set engraved gems into rings and pressed them into wax or clay, leaving a reversed seal for closing documents or marking identity. The British Museum holds a Roman gem showing an eagle, wreath, and palm branch. A tiny image like this could decorate a hand and travel with its owner as a personal signature.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_monte: Laurel wreaths recur on Roman imperial coin portraits, figures of Victory, and other images of success. The motif kept carrying victory and authority long after any single ceremony ended. Wherever the coins travelled, the laureate face of power travelled with them.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_many_: Roman military rites involved standards, emperors, and Jupiter. Soldiers might also honour hometown gods, local deities, Mithras, or others, with the mixture varying from camp to camp. The inscriptions leave too much variety for one war god to represent every Roman soldier.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.roman_games: A Roman fibula worked much like a safety pin: the pin and catch secured a cloak or garment, while metalwork, enamel, and varied shapes added decoration. By the Late Empire, gold crossbow fibulae could also signal senior military or administrative status. The same brooch could be an everyday fastening and a display of rank.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_mexic: Today, Aztec often serves as an umbrella term for related peoples and an empire in the Basin of Mexico. For inhabitants of Tenochtitlan, Mexica or Tenochca is often more precise. The names overlap, but they do not always cover the same people.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_macua: The macuahuitl had a wooden body lined with rows of obsidian blades. Obsidian fractures into an extremely sharp edge, but is more brittle than metal; damaged blades could be replaced. Almost no securely proven complete pre-conquest example survives, so modern reconstructions piece together images, written accounts, and lithic archaeology.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_china: This Mexica gold eagle head is a labret, or tentetl. Its stem passed through a piercing below the lower lip, leaving the eagle beside the mouth, where the metal beak would catch the eye during speech and movement. The Met links such lavish ornaments with elite power and military regalia.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_cacao: Costly gold labrets were not ornaments for everyone. A surviving eagle-head example puts precious metal, a predatory bird, and a permanent piercing directly on the face, publicly marking class and military identity. It shows how rank could be worn, without providing a universal ornament code for every military grade.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_feath: Obsidian often brings blades to mind, yet Mexica artisans also ground it into refined ear ornaments. A Met example preserves a broad disc and slender plug with a deep black polish. Hard, brittle, and reflective, volcanic glass still carried the visual force of a cutting material when worn on the body.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_offer: A Mexica obsidian mirror in the British Museum was carefully ground and polished on both faces, then drilled near the edge for suspension. Patient abrasion could make dark volcanic glass reflect a face. Here, obsidian became a complete mirror made to hang and be seen.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_warri: In the Codex Telleriano-Remensis, Tonatiuh has a red-and-yellow body, short white and long green feathers, jade and gold ornaments, and a red-feather solar emblem on his back. Colour, plumage, jewellery, and insignia build the whole image. Reducing him to a round sun face would lose most of those identifying details.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.aztec_huitz: Rain, Life, and a Greenstone Pendant

A Mexica greenstone rain-god pendant is pierced at the top for suspension. The Met notes that green stone evoked water, feathers, fertility, and precious things. Though the figure is small, its material already strengthens its connection to rain and life.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_giza_: Middle Kingdom protective wands were often carved from hippopotamus ivory, keeping the natural curve of the canine tooth. Craftspeople covered them with knife-bearing guardian beings; some inscriptions promise protection by day or night, and others name a child. The tooth of a dangerous animal became a tool for guarding birth and rebirth.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_chari: New Kingdom light chariots usually paired a driver with a warrior. The warrior shot a composite bow from the vehicle, while the chariot supplied speed, pursuit, and a display of authority. Temple reliefs make the pharaoh look unstoppable; they served royal representation and cannot be read as neutral snapshots of battle.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_faien: Wear the Moon on Your Head

Khonsu was an Egyptian moon god, often shown as a youthful deity wearing the lunar disk. Surviving gold pendants and Egyptian-blue shrines name him directly, while other small figures can be recognised by the disk, sidelock, and wrapped body. The god of the sky was reduced to a few centimetres, turning the moon into a portable amulet.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_ostra: Ancient Egyptians produced animal mummies in great numbers, and the sacred ibis was a common subject. Surviving examples use herringbone or geometric linen patterns, and some carry an applied image of a deity. The wrapping, materials, and remains inside each bundle all preserve clues to ritual practice.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_senet: Middle Kingdom fish ornaments were made from gold, green stone, or crystal, and some hung from the ends of braids worn by children or young women. Tilapia brood their eggs in the mouth until they hatch, helping the fish acquire associations with fertility and rebirth. A familiar Nile fish became a protective emblem worn close to the body.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_cats_: Cats were closely associated with Bastet, and large numbers of cat mummies were offered in worship. Living cats caught mice, rats, and snakes, and also became household companions. Gods, animal manifestations, temple animals, offerings, and pets occupied different roles; saying that Egyptians worshipped every cat blurs them together.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_arrow: Ancient Egyptian arrowheads were made from flint, bone, hardwood, copper, and bronze, with forms changing by period and purpose. Cheap, sharp stone remained in use after metal technology appeared. Real technologies rarely behave like a game tree where unlocking one material instantly deletes the old one.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.egypt_book_: Late Egyptian amulets often show Anubis as a jackal-headed man, with a hole or loop behind the head or back for suspension. His connection with mummification and protection of the dead made him well suited to a close-worn guardian. A god from large funerary rites was reduced to a figure small enough to carry.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_cross: A Warring States pendant set in the National Museum of China strings together agate rings, a coiled-serpent jade bi, jade kui-dragons, turquoise beads, and crystal beads at the waist. As the wearer walked, the pieces could lightly strike one another. In this set, the bi took part in ritual while moving with the body as a real ornament.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_terra: The terracotta figures from the mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor were originally covered with lacquer and bright pigments, including red, green, blue, purple, and white. After excavation, the sudden change of environment can make the fragile lacquer curl and the colours detach quickly. Their familiar clay colour is partly a result of preservation, not the original design.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_bambo: Before paper became widespread, scribes wrote on prepared strips of bamboo or wood and tied them into bundles. Once the cords decayed, the strips scattered, leaving archaeologists to reorder them through numbering, handwriting, size, and context. Excavated slips preserve laws, accounts, and letters, as well as versions of texts that can be compared with those handed down later.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_great: Some high-status Liangzhu burials placed as many as roughly forty jade bi beside one person. The discs sometimes lay in groups near the body alongside other jade ritual objects. One bi looks austere; repeated across a burial, the same shape magnifies wealth, rank, and ceremonial weight.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_ji_co: Many Han jade cicadas were han, mouth jades placed with the dead, rather than objects made for suspension. Palace Museum examples show that such cicadas often lack a hole and favour a flat, concise form. Distinguishing pendant, headdress fitting, and burial jade requires the perforations and archaeological context; silhouette alone is not enough.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_caval: Because cicadas emerge from the earth and shed their skins, Han burial practice could use them as images of renewal. A jade cicada in the National Museum of China was placed in the deceased's mouth, while perforated examples might serve as pendants or headdress ornaments. One small insect linked daily adornment with hopes for the afterlife.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_guand: Historical Chinese writers affectionately called cats linu, or “raccoon servants”. A painting traditionally attributed to a Song artist shows eight cats playing in a garden and even catches their pupils narrowed to slits at noon. A Ming Cat and Butterfly painting turns the shared sound of “cat and butterfly” and “advanced age” into a wish for longevity; the painted cats carry close observation and auspicious meaning together.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.china_guan_: Western Zhou jade fish often come from burials, with curved bodies and holes at the mouth or body for stringing alongside other beads and jades. The National Museum of China describes them as common ornaments of the period, especially in elite tombs. The simple little fish already had a long, well-documented tradition as something worn.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_bow_b: Early Samurai Were Known for Horse and Bow

Late Heian and Kamakura ideals often pictured the warrior as a mounted archer. Swords remained important, but never monopolised every battlefield in every century. As armies and tactics changed, spears, foot archery, and firearms grew prominent; imagining samurai as sword-only fighters leaves much of that history out.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_yari_: Sengoku yari came in many lengths and blade shapes, and were used by both foot soldiers and high-ranking warriors. Their long shafts extended reach and suited collective fighting. The sword remained useful for carrying, close combat, and displaying status, but large battlefields held far more than formal sword duels.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_laced: Early o-yoroi joined many small lames into sections, protected them with lacquer, and connected them with coloured lacing, producing something more flexible than a single iron shell. As warfare and firearms changed the demands of protection, later armour adopted larger plates, different fastenings, and even light folding forms that could be packed into a box.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_sword: Japanese smiths often signed the tang, the part hidden inside the hilt and normally unseen. Appraisers study inscriptions, file marks, holes, and natural patina. Some blades were never signed, and shortening an old sword could remove its original tang and signature together.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_daish: Kimono had no pockets, so small boxes and pouches hung from cords passed behind the obi. A netsuke at the cord's end caught against the sash like a toggle and counterweight, keeping the container from falling. It later developed into intricate miniature sculpture, turning a practical fitting into art worn at the waist.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_mongo: Mail Hid in Sleeves and Greaves

Mail in Japanese armour was often sewn into sleeves and greaves. British Museum examples combine iron links, small plates, and textile, keeping joints flexible while reinforcing vulnerable areas with hard pieces. It formed a connecting layer within the full armour system, with a structure different from a long European mail shirt.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_bushi: Bushido Was Never Set in Stone

Warriors in different periods discussed loyalty, honour, household survival, courage, and restraint, but the emphasis changed with warfare, lord-vassal relations, and social order. Edo thinkers and the modern state later reorganised and promoted bushido. Its history was repeatedly interpreted and rewritten; there was never one set of rules memorised by every samurai.
knowledge.echo_warrior.entry.japan_tomoe: Paper Figures Bore the Body's Ill Fortune

Japanese shrine purification can use a paper human figure. The worshipper rubs it against the body, breathes onto it, and leaves it with the shrine, symbolically transferring impurity or misfortune. The figure is not a combat substitute; it carries the ritual idea that another human-shaped form can receive what troubles a person.

gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.introduct: Echo Warrior is a mod about archaeology and summoned companions.
As you play, you will meet several powerful warriors from history.
Customize their skills and equipment to build an Echo of your own!
*You may also pick up a few interesting pieces of history along the way.
**A salvage device keeps both your inventory and base storage tidy.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.battlefie: Piglins and other otherworldly powers once invaded the Overworld again and again.
Across the long course of history, many civilizations rose to resist those invasions.
Their abandoned proof can still be found in ruined battlefields today.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.compass_a: Listen carefully to the sound it makes.
The Echo Compass points toward the nearest ruined battlefield.
Research suggests that it resonates with intent data attached to relics.
That is why it always leads to at least one Echo Relic.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.discoveri: A battlefield dig site usually contains one Echo Relic.
You may also find Knowledge Fragments, Legacies, and Echo Accessories.
Other supplies left on the battlefield may still be useful.
You might even uncover proof that a Nether army was defeated!
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.knowledge: Loose pages recording all kinds of small facts.
Reading one gives you knowledge—the kind in your head, not experience points or research currency.
Combine fragments freely into a collection for easier reading and a much happier inventory.
A collection can hold duplicates of the same fragment.
Fragments can be removed at any time, so store them without worry.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.legacy.bo: Even in different eras, the same bright qualities can deserve to be carried onward.
Heroic accounts can be found while excavating ruins or visiting village libraries. Reading them grants a benefit.
They are also ingredients for accessories that embody their virtues.
Too many duplicate fragments or accessories you no longer need?
Craft a Salvage Chest and place them inside.
YMC.Inc collects the contents at midnight
and returns some raw materials in exchange.
Note: only content from this mod can be salvaged.
Scan relic data and reconstruct an Echo Warrior projection.
Right-click to load a relic and fuel, equip accessories, and configure skills.
Rotten flesh and soul sand provide fuel.
Only one copy of each accessory may be installed.
No strange visions or causal problems. Promise.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.roman_leg: A formidable Roman legionary whose sturdy shield greatly reduces damage from the front.
He draws enemy attention and answers it with a spectacular counterattack.
His aura strengthens nearby allies, especially allies forming a shield wall.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.aztec_war: A powerful Aztec warrior blessed by the gods.
The warrior shares divine favor with the summoner.
A sweeping macuahuitl cuts flesh and causes bleeding.
He leaps toward enemies with divine force, bringing fear and an ending.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.egyptian_: A mobile and adaptable Egyptian archer.
Devotion to the cat goddess makes this Echo a natural foe of creepers and undead.
Special arrows, chariots, and volleys provide agile movement and multiple shots.
When threatened, a backstep volley creates an emergency escape.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.guandao_w: An unyielding warrior from ancient China.
Heavy armor resists knockback and projectiles.
Attack and defense build steadily during battle.
Elaborate guandao forms control large groups of enemies.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.japanese_: A Japanese samurai who has entered a state of flow.
The samurai pursues enemies while evading their attacks.
Recent attacks and low health raise the chance to dodge.
Skills close the distance before a spectacular, lethal thrust.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.page.accessori: Every civilization has its own artifacts, cultural objects, and works of skilled hands.
Find them in battlefields or craft them from records preserved in Legacies.
Accessories improve Echoes, but only one copy of each name can be installed.
gui.echo_warrior.tutorial.thanks:
Thank you for reading
and playing
